newsitem.title: USA: Savings opportunities for Medicare beneficiaries.
newsitem.headline: Savings opportunities for Medicare beneficiaries.

text.p: Medicare beneficiaries have a few new opportunities for saving money, thanks to this week's budget agreement and an unrelated comparison-shopping service offered by a private insurance rating firm.
The new tax law will offer Medigap policy buyers the chance to save for their premiums and out-of-pocket costs in a new pilot pre-tax savings account, called a medical savings account.

It will also throw some money at Medicare-supplementing health maintenence organisations in an effort to lure them to rural areas, and will offer new coverage for preventive health care, including cancer and osteoporosis screening.

The price-shopping service, by Weiss Ratings Inc., in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., offers safety ratings and price-comparison charts on the Medigap policies that most Medicare enrollees buy to supplement their coverage.
It really pays to comparison shop for those policies. In its survey of 153 insurers, Weiss found huge price discrepancies among plans offering identical coverage to identical individuals.
You can pay as much as $1,800 more than your neighbour for the same plan if you don't shop around.

Why? According to Martin Weiss, chairman of the firm, some companies are trying to buy Medigap business while others may be trying to leave certain markets. Because of that, there is no correlation between the quality of the company offering the plan, the service offered by the company and the amount the company charges. There's no reason not to go for a low-priced policy, as long as it is offered by a solid, financially secure company.

Medigap insurance is designed to fill the numerous gaps of Medicare coverage, such as lengthy hospital stays, foreign health care, prescriptions, dental care, many immunisations, eyeglasses, hearing aids and hospital extras such as private rooms with telephones and televisions.

Medigap plans are issued by private insurance companies, but their benefits are set by law. There are 10 different levels of Medigap policy, ranging from a bare bones "A" level to the Cadiallac of Medigap: "J" policies that cover high prescription costs, preventive care, at-home recovery, foreign travel and nursing home recuperation benefits, as well as Medicare deductibles and co-insurance. In between "A" and "J" are eight other policies that offer graduated benefits.

Medicare enrollees should decide what level of Medigap coverage they want and can afford and then shop for the best price in that level. According to Weiss, for example, a Florida shopper looking for a "J" plan could find discrepancies as high as $1,810 for plans with the same list of benefits. Maryland shoppers could pay as little as $360 a year with USAA Life Insurance Company or as much as $772 a year for the same plan offered by Blue Cross & Blue Shield National Capital Area.
Shoppers can get a customised local list of plans, their safety ratings and prices for $39 from Weiss by dialing (800) 289-9222.

As for the Medical Savings Accounts established by the new legislation, it may take them a while to show up, and they will most likely be offered directly by insurance companies, just as the current savings accounts for self-employed workers are offered. These accounts allow tax deductions for contributions to medical savings accounts that can be used to pay health care premiums or out-of-pocket costs. The money in those accounts can accumulate tax-free for years as long as it is eventually used for medical purposes.

You can e-mail Linda Stern at 72160.1546(at)compuserve.com or write to her in care of Reuters, Suite 410, 1333 H St., NW, Washington, DC 20005. She regrets that she cannot answer each letter individually, but will cover your questions in upcoming columns.
